identity.title: AKT as a central node integrating multidrug resistance mechanisms in ovarian Cancer.

content.abstract: Ovarian cancer, particularly high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC), remains a leading cause of gynecologic cancer mortality. Although HGSOC responds to platinum-taxane therapy, 70-85% relapse, with acquired resistance playing a major role. The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT)/mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, centered on AKT, contributes to this resistance. Current literature examines AKT's downstream consequences in isolation, overlooking their collective contribution to tumor evolution; this review addresses that gap by separating upstream AKT activation from downstream resistance outputs. Intrinsic genomic alterations (PIK3CA mutation, phosphatase and tensin homolog [PTEN] loss) and extrinsic tumor microenvironment (TME) cues converge on AKT, which drives four emerging resistance mechanisms (metabolic reprogramming and ferroptosis evasion, epigenetic modulation of homologous recombination inhibitor sensitivity, cancer stem cell plasticity, and immune evasion, discussed with therapeutic targeting), integrated with classical mechanisms into a unified chemoresistance framework. AKT promotes chemoresistance by coordinating ATP-binding cassette transporter-mediated drug efflux, RAD51/BRCA-dependent DNA repair, and an elevated apoptotic threshold via Bcl-2-associated agonist of cell death and survivin modulation. Spatial organization and interconnections are highlighted, including amplified AKT activation at the tumor-stromal interface through cancer-associated fibroblast-derived exosomal PTEN silencing. We evaluate therapeutic strategies (AKT and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors, folate receptor alpha-targeted antibody-drug conjugates such as mirvetuximab soravtansine, and metabolic modulation through the AKT/mTORC1 axis) by targeting multiple nodes simultaneously. Patient-derived organoids, CRISPR/Cas9 screening, and circulating tumor DNA monitoring enable clinical translation, supporting rationally designed combinations over sequential monotherapy and reframing AKT from a poor-prognosis marker to a therapeutic target in recurrent, chemoresistant ovarian cancer.
